messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi had always found solace in his work as a painter. The smell of turpentine and oil paints, the feel of a brush in his hand, it all seemed to calm his mind. But that was before his wife, Ama, passed away suddenly. It's been two years now, but Kofi still finds himself waking up in the dead of night, his body tense and ready to react to danger. He can't shake off the feeling of being on guard, even inside his own home. It started with the ambulance that took Ama away. The sound of its sirens still haunts him, making him feel like he's constantly waiting for another tragedy to strike. Whenever he hears an ambulance outside his studio, Kofi's mind starts racing and his body goes into high alert. He tries to distract himself by focusing on his work, but the memories come flooding back - images of Ama's lifeless body, the feeling of emptiness that consumed him. He can't help but wonder if he could have done something to prevent her death. The memories are always there, lurking just beneath the surface. Sometimes Kofi feels like he's drowning in grief, overwhelmed by emotions that he can't quite explain. Other times, it's as if his mind is a blank slate, devoid of any clear images or memories. But the pain is always there, gnawing away at him. Kofi's friends and family have tried to be supportive, but he feels isolated and set apart from others. He struggles to connect with them, to find meaning in a world that seems to have lost all sense. His work, once his passion, now feels like a chore. He goes through the motions, but it's all just a reminder of what he's lost. As Kofi navigates this new reality, he finds himself on edge more often than not. The slightest noise can startle him, and he's constantly looking over his shoulder, waiting for something to go wrong. His body is always tense, ready to react to danger that may or may not be there. And when the memories come flooding back, Kofi feels like he's losing himself all over again. The triggers are everywhere - in the ambulance sirens, in the conversations about loss and grief, even in his own workspace. They bring back the memories, which in turn fuel his feelings of threat and danger. It's a vicious cycle that Kofi can't seem to break free from. He feels like he's lost himself, like his life has been destroyed by the trauma. Despite all this, Kofi still holds onto hope. He hopes that one day he'll find a way to manage his symptoms, to learn to live with the memories without being consumed by them. For now, though, the pain and fear remain, a constant reminder of what he's lost. What brought Kofi to seek help was the realization that he couldn't keep living like this. He wants to be able to connect with others again, to find meaning in his work and his life. Most of all, he wants to be able to remember Ama without feeling overwhelmed by grief and pain.
